slides.text: Julian was the city’s premier acoustic forensic analyst, capable of identifying the caliber of a firearm or the engine block of a getaway van from a three-second surveillance clip. When billionaire Arthur Vance was found shot dead inside his soundproof penthouse panic room, detectives were baffled. The heavy vault door had been bolted from within; the lone security microphone captured only forty seconds of silence before the fatal blast. Police ruled it an airtight suicide. Julian was not convinced.

Isolating the audio track through an analog spectral analyzer, Julian stripped away the air conditioning hum and magnified the background waveform by six hundred percent. Underneath the apparent silence, a rhythmic, microtonal pulse emerged—not human breathing, but the distinctive, rapid flutter of a shutter mechanism from an antique Hasselblad camera. Someone hadn't broken into the panic room to assassinate Vance. Vance had sealed himself inside specifically to be photographed doing something he couldn't survive.

Julian enhanced the tiny audio reflection bouncing off the vault’s bulletproof glass. In the final second before the gun fired, a synthesized text-to-speech voice whispered from a hidden speaker: 'Smile for your shareholders, Arthur.' Julian froze. That wasn't a suicide; it was an execution by blackmail, triggered remotely via an acoustic frequency. And as Julian went to save the waveform to a flash drive, his own laboratory speakers suddenly clicked on, humming the exact same pitch.
